**Cover letter: Data Scientist, Demand Forecasting, Waypoint Mobility**

---

Dear Waypoint Mobility Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Scientist, Demand Forecasting role on your Forecasting team. I've spent most of the last three years working with transit ridership data, first as an analyst at a regional transit agency and then as a research assistant building ridership forecasting models. I'd like to keep doing that work on a platform that planners in 40+ cities use.

At Lakeshore University's Urban Analytics Lab, I built XGBoost and LightGBM models for bus ridership. I used four years of automatic passenger counter data joined with anonymized mobility data, and I led the feature engineering and evaluation. Against a SARIMA baseline, the model cut MAPE from 14.2% to 9.8% on a 2023 holdout. A reviewer was concerned that the lagged mobility features leaked future information, so I re-ran the model with a longer lag. MAPE rose to 10.4%, which still clearly beat the baseline. That experience taught me to build evaluations that hold up under scrutiny, not just ones that produce good numbers. The work became a first-author paper at the UrbanDS 2025 workshop, and I presented it there.

Before graduate school, I was a Data Analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the SQL and Tableau ridership dashboards that the planning department used, and I automated the weekly reporting pipeline in Python, cutting preparation time from about six hours to one. That job showed me what planners actually need from a number: something they can trust and explain to their board. I also learned to redesign dashboards for non-technical readers.

This summer, as a Data Science Intern at Northpoint Insurance, I built a gradient-boosted churn model that raised validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76 over the existing baseline, and I calibrated its probabilities with isotonic regression. I presented the results to the retention team and a VP in business terms, focusing on which segments the model flags and how outreach could be prioritized. The model was handed off for further evaluation. I haven't yet taken a model all the way to production, and working with your engineers to do that is one of the things that draws me to this role.

I finish my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore in December 2026, and I'm excited about Waypoint because the work stays close to transit. I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I could help improve your forecasts at the stop, route, and network level.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Morgan Reyes

---

I wrote this letter from scratch rather than reusing the HealthBridge one. That letter has two claims I left out on purpose:

- **"Peer-reviewed paper":** your CV lists the paper as a non-archival workshop paper, so I called it a workshop paper.
- **"Over 30%" error reduction:** I gave the exact MAPE numbers instead. The 30% figure only holds for the one-week-lag model (the two-week version is about 27%).

I also left out your PhD application, since it could raise questions about whether you'd stay.

I wrote your Khoury statement from your CV and our past chats.

**Statement of Interest: PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

---

Last spring, I watched a classmate train a model in an AutoML dashboard, accept the top-ranked result, and move on. She never looked at its metrics. Neither did most of the other participants in our usability study. None of the five opened the feature-importance panel, and two assumed the tool already "knew" which columns were sensitive and had handled them. These were data science graduate students, the people best placed to question the tool. That study changed my question. I had been asking how to build a more accurate model. Now I want to know how people decide what to trust in a model's output, and how tools could support that judgment rather than replace it. I am applying to the HCI PhD program at Khoury to study that question properly.

**How I got here**

I came to this question through the people who use models, not through modeling itself. After a B.A. in Economics, I worked for a year as a data analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained ridership dashboards for the planning department and automated our weekly reporting pipeline. The technical work went well, but the hardest problem was making the numbers usable. When I was asked to adapt a dashboard for board members, I had to rethink what it showed: which comparisons mattered, what to cut, and how to show uncertainty without inviting false precision. A chart I found obvious was not obvious to the people making service decisions from it.

In my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University, I joined Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab as a research assistant, building gradient-boosted models to forecast bus ridership recovery. I led the feature engineering and evaluation and wrote the first draft of our paper, which I presented at the UrbanDS 2025 workshop. The revision process taught me more than the modeling did. A reviewer asked whether our lagged mobility features leaked future information. I re-ran the analysis with a longer lag and reported the weaker result alongside the original. I learned that a credible claim depends on anticipating how a skeptical reader will test it. But when I presented the work, the questions I found most interesting were not about MAPE. They were about whether a transit planner would actually change a decision based on a forecast, and what they would need to see first.

I saw the same gap in industry. As a data science intern at Northpoint Insurance, I built a churn model and presented it to the retention team and a VP. Most of my preparation went into explaining what an AUC of 0.76 does and does not mean for deciding who to call. As a teaching assistant for STAT 1100, a statistics course for non-majors, I helped write a grading rubric in which "interpretation" was a separate criterion from "analysis." The most common weak answers came from students who ran the right test and then drew a conclusion the result did not support.

**What I want to study**

Across these settings, the hardest problem was what happened between a model's output and a human decision. I want to study that space empirically and design for it. Directions that interest me:

- **Calibrated reliance on automated data tools.** Our AutoML study was small and unpublished: five participants in a course project. Still, it suggested that users read a tool's polish as competence, including competence it did not have. I would like to study when and why users defer to AutoML and AI-assisted analysis tools, and which interface interventions lead them to check, question, or override the system.
- **Communicating uncertainty to decision-makers.** Planners, managers, and the public routinely act on forecasts and risk scores. I am interested in how forecast uncertainty can be presented so that non-specialists make better decisions with it, rather than ignoring it or being paralyzed by it.

My training is mostly quantitative, and I know I still need to build depth in qualitative and design methods. The think-aloud study was my first real exposure to them, and it is a large part of why I want a PhD rather than another modeling role. I bring experience building, evaluating, and deploying the kinds of models whose users I want to study, and I know firsthand where those models' outputs get misread.

**Why Khoury**

Khoury's HCI group combines human-centered research with deep technical work on AI systems, which is the combination my questions need. I am particularly interested in working with **[Faculty Name]**, whose work on **[specific topic/paper]** connects to my interest in **[link]**, and with **[Faculty Name 2]**, whose **[topic]** relates to **[link]**. Boston's dense network of transit agencies and civic-tech organizations would also offer research partners whose decisions depend on data tools.

I finish my M.S. in December 2026. I want to spend the next several years working out how people come to trust the tools I have spent the last several years building, and how to design those tools so that trust is earned.

---

**What you need to fill in:**

- **Faculty names (required).** I left placeholders rather than guess at fit. Please read two or three recent papers from each person before naming them.
- **A privacy angle you could add.** During the RA project, you looked into how the vendor's mobility data was collected and said, "I doubt anyone tapping 'allow' pictured this." Together with the two AutoML participants who assumed the tool handled sensitive data, that could support a privacy and consent thread. Tianshi Li's PEACH Lab at Khoury works on HCI, AI, and privacy, so it would give you a natural faculty match. I didn't include this because it was an offhand comment, not a stated research interest. Also, describing the lab's data practices critically might be awkward since Prof. Patel is writing one of your letters. If it reflects how you actually feel, I can draft that paragraph.
- **Accuracy check.** I described the AutoML study as small and unpublished, and I left out the PhD-vs-job uncertainty. Please check that "Last spring" and the participant details match how you'd tell the story.

I’m an Assistant Professor at Northeastern University in the Khoury College of Computer Sciences, directing the PEACH (Privacy-Enabling AI and Computer-Human interaction) Lab . I’m also a core faculty member at the Cybersecurity and Privacy Institute at Northeastern University. I earned my PhD from Carnegie Mellon University and my Bachelor of Science degree from Peking University.

My work is driven by the belief that privacy sustains human agency, safe exploration, and free expression in a connected world. My interest focuses on studying and addressing the emerging LLM privacy issues from a human-centered perspective . Check out our position paper for an overview of the important and understudied problems and the research agenda. Below are a sample of topics I’m actively exploring with my students and collaborators:

Data minimization in LLM systems "It's a Fair Game", or Is It? How Users Navigate Disclosure Risks and Benefits in LLM Chatbots (CHI'24)

Rescriber: User-Led Data Minimization for Chatbots, Powered by Smaller LLMs (CHI'25)

The Obvious Invisible Threat: GUI Agents' Vulnerability to Fine-Print Injections (TAISAP'26)

Human Oversight of Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents

Comparing Human Oversight Strategies for Computer-Use Agents

CIDER: Contextual Disclosure Boundaries for Privacy Preference Alignment (COLM'26)

Disclose with Care: Designing Privacy Controls in Interview Chatbots

My broad research interests lie at the intersection of HCI, Privacy, and AI. I strive to address the increasing privacy issues in today’s digital world using a blend of human-centered problem understanding and technical problem solving. I conduct mixed-methods research to understand the privacy challenges situated in different stakeholders’ lived experiences, and develop models and systems to tackle these problems.

My research and expert commentary have been featured in MIT Technology Review , The Washington Post , WIRED , New Scientist , POLITICO , The Straits Times , and Consumer Reports , among others.

The work from my lab has been generously funded by NSF, Google, and Samsung.

I rewrote the statement around privacy, with the trust material now in a supporting role. I also took out "deploying." I checked Tianshi Li's current publications to tailor the Khoury section.

**Statement of Interest: PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

---

As a research assistant forecasting bus ridership, I spent an afternoon testing a feature that never made it into our model. I combined two columns from our anonymized data: the stop where a frequent rider usually first boarded, and the area where their phone usually was at night. Neither column seemed revealing alone. Together, they narrowed many riders down to just a few city blocks. The feature didn't improve the model, so I dropped it, and nothing about our project was out of line. But I kept thinking about where the second column came from. The mobility data came from software in partner apps, where people had given one-time consent by tapping "allow." I doubt anyone who tapped it pictured a graduate student, years later, inferring roughly where they sleep. And as far as I know, they had no way to find out it was possible.

Since then, I have kept coming back to two questions. What do people believe can be inferred from the data they share? And could they ever see what is actually inferred? These questions matter even more now that people share far more with AI tools they talk to than they ever did with a transit app. I am applying to the HCI PhD program at Khoury to study them.

**How I got here**

My background is in quantitative work. After a B.A. in Economics, I spent a year as a data analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained ridership dashboards for planners and automated our weekly reporting pipeline. Redesigning a dashboard for board members taught me early that data is only as useful as people's understanding of it.

In my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University, I joined Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab. There I built gradient-boosted models on four years of passenger counter data joined with anonymized mobility data, and wrote the first draft of a first-author paper that I presented at the UrbanDS 2025 workshop. That work gave me a practitioner's view of how personal data is used in research. I know which joins are easy, which features get explored and quietly dropped, and how far "anonymized" data is from anonymous once it is combined with other data. The revision process also shaped how I do research. A reviewer suspected that our lagged mobility features leaked future information, so I re-ran the analysis with a longer lag and reported the weaker result alongside the original. I want to bring the same habit of testing my own claims to studying people.

My first real HCI research was a usability study in a Human-Centered Data Science course. My team of three ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates using an AutoML tool. Most participants accepted the top-ranked model without checking its metrics. Two of them assumed the tool "knew" which columns were sensitive and had handled them. It hadn't. These were data science graduate students, and even they held a confident, wrong mental model of what an automated system knew about their data. The study was small and unpublished, but it showed me that the gap I had seen from the data side could be studied directly, by watching how people reason about what a system can see and do.

I have also spent much of my time translating between technical results and the people who act on them. At Northpoint Insurance, I presented a churn model to a VP and the retention team. As a teaching assistant for a statistics course for non-majors, I helped design a rubric that graded interpretation separately from analysis. Both experiences sharpened my interest in how people form beliefs about what data reveals.

**What I want to study**

I am most interested in the gap between what people think they are disclosing and what can be inferred from it. Directions I would like to pursue:

- **Mental models of inference.** When people share location with an app or personal details with a chatbot, what do they believe a system or a determined analyst could infer, especially from combining their data with other sources? Where are those beliefs most wrong, and does it matter for what they choose to share?
- **Making inference visible.** Consent is usually collected once, up front, about data rather than about inferences. I want to explore interfaces that show people what their disclosures make possible, in a form they can act on, and test whether that changes their decisions.
- **Disclosure to AI tools.** Conversational AI invites people to share more context than any form ever asked for. I want to study how people decide what to share with these tools, and how the tools themselves could help people share less without making them less useful.

I know my methods training is weighted toward modeling, and I want to build real depth in qualitative and experimental methods. I think my technical background will help with research on inference, because I have built the kinds of pipelines whose inferences I want to make visible.

**Why Khoury**

I am especially interested in working with **Prof. Tianshi Li** and the PEACH Lab. Her CHI 2024 study of how users navigate disclosure risks with LLM-based chatbots found that people's mental models and the systems' design limited their awareness of privacy risks. That is very close to the question I want to pursue. Rescriber's approach of user-led data minimization is the kind of work I hope to do: tools that give people perceptible control over what they disclose. Her recent position paper with Niloofar Mireshghallah argues that inference attacks and data aggregation are understudied relative to memorization. My afternoon with two "anonymized" columns was a small, concrete instance of exactly that problem. **[Optional: a second faculty member and one sentence on fit.]**

I finish my M.S. in December 2026. I have spent several years on the analyst's side of personal data. I want to spend the next several working on the side of the people the data comes from, helping them understand what their data can reveal before they share it.

The question I keep coming back to started with a feature I threw away.

I was a research assistant on a bus ridership project, and one afternoon I tried combining two columns from our anonymized data: the stop where a regular rider usually got on, and where their phone usually was at night. Together, those two columns put a lot of riders on just a few blocks. The feature didn't help the model, so I deleted it, and that was the end of it as far as the project was concerned. Nobody had done anything wrong.

But I couldn't stop thinking about it. The phone data came from partner apps, where people had tapped "allow" once. I doubt anyone tapping "allow" pictured this. I didn't think they were careless. I thought there was no way for them to know. What can be inferred from data depends on what it's combined with, by whom, and years later. None of that is visible when you tap the button, and as far as I could tell, it never becomes visible afterward.

That afternoon gave me two questions I still have. What do people think can be inferred from what they share? And could they ever actually see what is inferred? Since then, the questions have grown, because people now share things with AI tools they talk to that they would never have typed into a form. They tell a chatbot about their health, their job, their relationships, often in passing, to get a better answer. I want to understand what people imagine is happening to that information, where that picture is wrong, and whether a tool could show them, honestly and in a way they could act on.

I came to these questions from the other side of the data. I've spent most of my working life on the analyst's end: first at a regional transit agency, then in a research lab, now in a data science master's program. I know how easy a join is. But I've noticed that what I care about has been moving away from the model and toward the people around it. The clearest moment came in a Human-Centered Data Science course last spring. My team ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates using an AutoML tool. Two of them assumed the tool "knew" which columns were sensitive and had taken care of them. It hadn't. These were data science students, people who should have known better, and they still assumed the system understood their data better than it did. It was a small class project, but it was the first time I had studied how people think about data rather than the data itself. I didn't want to stop.

I'm early in this, and I know it. My training is mostly in statistics and modeling. I've run one small qualitative study, and I want to learn to do interviews, experiments, and design work properly, not just bolt them onto quantitative analysis. That's a large part of why I'm applying for a PhD rather than another job building models.

I'm especially drawn to Prof. Tianshi Li's work at the PEACH Lab. Her study of how people navigate disclosure in LLM chatbots ("It's a Fair Game," CHI 2024) asks very nearly the question I've been carrying around. Rescriber, a tool that helps people decide what to remove from their prompts before sending them, is the kind of thing I'd want to build: something that gives people real control in the moment they're sharing. Her recent argument that inference and data aggregation get far less research attention than they deserve described my afternoon with two "anonymized" columns better than I could.

I don't know yet exactly what my dissertation will be. I do know which question I want to spend the next five years on: how to help people see what their data reveals before someone else does.

Position: LLM Privacy Requires a Lifecycle-Wide Approach

Niloofar Mireshghallah † , Tianshi Li †

NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track)

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while a constellation of more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. This position paper argues that the privacy landscape of LLM systems extends far beyond training data extraction, encompassing risks from data collection practices, inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent capabilities, and the democratization of surveillance through deep inference attacks. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of privacy risks across the LLM lifecycle -- from data collection through deployment -- and demonstrate through case studies how current privacy frameworks fail to address these multifaceted threats. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,322 AI/ML privacy papers published at leading conferences over the past decade (2016--2025), we reveal that while memorization receives outsized attention in technical research, the most pressing privacy harms lie elsewhere, where current technical approaches offer little traction and viable paths forward remain unclear. We call for a fundamental shift in how the research community approaches LLM privacy, moving beyond the narrow focus of current technical solutions and embracing interdisciplinary approaches that address the sociotechnical nature of these emerging threats.

Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search

Jianing Wen, Tianshi Li

Preprint

As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDoxx, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents

Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li

COLM 2026

LLM agents require personal information for personalization in order to effectively act on users' behalf, but this raises privacy concerns that can discourage data sharing, limiting both the autonomy levels at which agents can operate and the effectiveness of personalization. Yet the expanded design space of agent autonomy also presents opportunities to shape these effects, which remain underexplored. We conducted a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) to study how agent autonomy level influences personalization's effects on users' privacy concerns, trust, and willingness to use, as well as the underlying psychological processes. We find that risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent delegates control back to users upon detecting potential privacy leakage, improves users' perceived control. This in turn attenuates personalization's adverse effects: privacy concerns rise less and trust declines less. Our results suggest that designing agent's autonomy that supports human autonomy (both perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns. This positions aligning decision authority between users and agents (autonomy alignment) as an important opportunity and challenge for trustworthy human-agent interaction.
